design_detail: Scientific statement of the American Heart Association, written by the Acute Cardiac Care Committee of the Council on Clinical Cardiology: a consensus document, not a systematic review. Eleven named cardiologists and emergency physicians reviewed the literature on cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction and issued diagnostic and therapeutic recommendations graded in the ACC/AHA format (Class I, IIa, IIb, III; Level of Evidence A, B, C). The writing committee describes a comprehensive search of English-language publications on humans and animals from 1960 to 2007, with broad searching on cocaine plus targeted searches on named topics, citations generally limited to articles listed in Index Medicus; no databases, search strings, selection criteria or study flow are given. Approved by the AHA Science Advisory and Coordinating Committee on 20 December 2007 and reviewed by outside reviewers nominated by the AHA. This is the document that carries the Class III recommendation against beta blockers in the acute setting, and the single table on p. 1902 states the kind and the size of the evidence behind each recommendation.
can_establish: What the American Heart Association recommended in 2008 for cocaine-associated chest pain and myocardial infarction, how it graded each recommendation, and, uniquely among such documents, how many patients and what kinds of study lay behind each therapy, including the 30 and 15 patients behind the Class III recommendations against beta blockers and labetalol.
cannot_establish: Whether any of the recommended or discouraged treatments changes patient outcomes. The statement generates no data, appraises no study formally, and says itself that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated myocardial infarction exists. Its Class III judgments are Level of Evidence C, which in its own definitions means consensus opinion, case studies or standard of care.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a consensus statement. The literature cited was gathered by the writing committee from a search of English-language human and animal publications from 1960 to 2007, with citations generally limited to articles listed in Index Medicus (p. 1897).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No inclusion or exclusion criteria for studies are stated and no study flow is reported. Targeted searches are listed for myocardial infarction, chest pain, emergency department, aspirin, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blocker, benzodiazepine, thrombolytics, phentolamine, heparin, primary angioplasty, electrocardiography and stress testing; beta blockers and labetalol, the two therapies given Class III recommendations, do not appear among the named targeted searches (p. 1897).
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The populations described are those of the cited studies, chiefly young urban patients: in the Cocaine-Associated Myocardial Infarction series of 130 patients, mean age 38 years, 72% non-white, 91% smokers, 88% with cocaine use in the preceding 24 hours (p. 1899).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence was selected by the committee without stated criteria, from English-language sources, and the search closed in 2007, before any of the hospital cohorts that later examined beta-blocker outcomes had been published. Several of the central citations on incidence, prognosis and chest-pain-unit management are studies co-authored by one member of the writing group. The disclosure table shows extensive industry relationships across the writing group, chiefly with diagnostic and cardiovascular-drug companies; this is recorded as a flag, and the therapies at issue here are generic.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no primary data). The statement reviews how cocaine use is ascertained in practice: self-report, or qualitative immunoassay for urinary benzoylecgonine above a usual cut-off of 300 ng/mL, detectable for about 24 to 48 hours after use, with a mean time to first negative specimen of 43.6 +/- 17.1 hours (range 16 to 66) in 18 people who had used cocaine intranasally, and detection as late as 22 days in people using large amounts long-term (p. 1899).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported only as the conditions of cited studies: the catheterization-laboratory studies gave intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (p. 1903).
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed qualitatively: alcohol intensifies the chronotropic effects of cocaine, and cocaine combined with cigarette smoking produces greater increases in heart rate and vasoconstriction than either alone (p. 1898).

comparison.controls: Not applicable: a consensus statement with no comparison group. The implicit comparator throughout is the management of acute coronary syndrome unrelated to cocaine, from which the statement departs in naming the exceptions (pp. 1901-1902).

outcomes.instruments: The ACC/AHA classification of recommendations and levels of evidence, defined on p. 1897: Class I beneficial and effective, Class II conflicting evidence or divergent opinion (IIa weight of evidence in favour, IIb usefulness less well established), Class III evidence or general agreement that the treatment is not useful and in some cases may be harmful; Level A from multiple randomized trials, Level B from a single randomized trial or non-randomized studies, Level C from consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care.
outcomes.validity_norms: No formal risk-of-bias appraisal of any cited study. The statement's substitute, and its most useful feature for a reader weighing the recommendations, is the table on p. 1902, which marks for each therapy which kinds of evidence exist (controlled clinical trials, cardiac catheterization laboratory studies, case series or observational studies, case reports, controlled in vivo animal experiments) and gives the total number of patients in the studies and reports behind it.
outcomes.operationalization: Recommendations are about acute hospital management; 'harm' for the Class III judgments is operationalized as worsening coronary vasoconstriction and, in animal models, decreased coronary blood flow, increased seizure frequency and increased mortality (p. 1902).

analysis.effect_sizes: No synthesis or pooling. The statement reports figures from individual sources: myocardial infarction in 6% of patients presenting with chest pain after cocaine use in the COCHPA study (246 patients) and in a retrospective urban series, against 0.7% in the ACI-TIPI study (293 patients) and 2.8% in a series of 218, an overall range of 0.7% to 6% (p. 1898). Of 130 patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction, 38% had cardiac complications, with heart failure in 7% and arrhythmias in up to 43% (ventricular tachycardia 18%, supraventricular tachycardia 5%, bradyarrhythmia 20%), 90% of complications within the first 12 hours and in-hospital mortality of 0% (p. 1899). In a chest-pain-unit study of 344 patients, 42 high-risk patients were admitted directly, of whom 10 (24%) had myocardial infarction and 10 (24%) unstable angina; of 302 intermediate- to low-risk patients observed, 4 of 256 (2%) sustained a non-fatal infarction and no cardiovascular deaths occurred, and of 158 who had a stress test before discharge 4 (3%) were positive (p. 1901). The electrocardiogram in COCHPA had a sensitivity of 36% and a specificity of 89.9% for true myocardial infarction, with positive predictive value 17.9% and negative predictive value 95.8% (p. 1900). Intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg narrowed coronary arterial diameter by 13% and phentolamine returned it to baseline (p. 1903). No confidence intervals accompany any of these figures except the sensitivity and specificity of rest perfusion imaging (100%, 95% CI 50% to 100%, and 99%, 95% CI 96% to 100%; p. 1900).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a scientific statement; no protocol or registration, and the ACC/AHA grading is applied by committee judgment.
analysis.selective_reporting: The table on p. 1902 is unusually candid about what the recommendations rest on, and the therapeutics section opens by stating that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated myocardial infarction has been reported. Against that, the beta-blocker section describes the catheterization evidence without saying that its participants had never used cocaine, that the propranolol was given directly into the coronary artery, or that only 10 and 9 people respectively received the drugs after cocaine (editors' observation from the cited studies, read in the same session).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The statement's own table shows that of the seven therapies considered for initial management, only benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin have any controlled clinical trial evidence, and that the recommendations against beta blockers and against labetalol rest on cardiac catheterization studies, case reports and animal experiments covering 30 and 15 patients respectively, with no controlled clinical trial and no observational study. Both are graded Level of Evidence C, which the statement defines as consensus opinion, case studies or standard of care.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The statement recommends that beta-adrenergic antagonists be avoided in the acute setting (Class III) and that labetalol offers no advantage (Class III), reinforcing these with quotations from two earlier guidelines, one stating that beta blockers should not be given in cocaine-precipitated ST-elevation infarction because of the risk of exacerbating coronary spasm, the other that propranolol is contraindicated in cocaine overdose. The gap is not between the data and the recommendation, which the committee grades honestly as Level C, but in what travels afterwards: a Class III recommendation in an American Heart Association statement is read as settled, while the document itself shows it rests on two small catheterization studies in patients who had never used cocaine, one of which gave the drug directly into a coronary artery. The statement also argues the risk-benefit balance explicitly and well, noting that beta blockers lower mortality after ordinary infarction but that deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, so the balance differs. The discharge recommendation is appropriately conditional, reserving long-term beta blockers for documented infarction, left ventricular systolic dysfunction or ventricular arrhythmias, individualized and with counselling about recurrent cocaine use.

timeline.event: Intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow in 10 of 30 cocaine-naive catheterization patients: the human evidence behind the Class III recommendation
Intravenous labetalol in 9 of 15 similar patients lowered arterial pressure without relieving coronary vasoconstriction: the human evidence behind the labetalol recommendation
This statement, approved December 2007, grades both beta blockers and labetalol Class III, Level of Evidence C
Retrospective cohort of 376 patients finds no detectable difference in in-hospital outcomes with or without a beta blocker, and notes that 44% received one despite the recommendation
Meta-analysis of five retrospective cohorts finds no significant pooled difference in infarction or death and suggests the guidelines be reconsidered

replication.where_it_stands: The statement's literature search closed in 2007, so none of the hospital cohorts that later examined outcomes could be considered. Those cohorts have not shown the harm the mechanism predicts, but they are non-randomized, treated patients were systematically sicker, and no randomized trial has been done. As of the present reading the Class III recommendation stands in the guidelines while the observational literature pulls against it, and both sides rest on evidence the editors of this encyclopedia rate as weak.

funding.funder: No external funding is reported for the statement; it is a product of the American Heart Association, which states it makes every effort to avoid actual or potential conflicts of interest among writing-panel members (p. 1897).
funding.declared_conflicts: A full disclosure table for the writing group is printed on p. 1904. Seven of the eleven members declare relationships; those marked significant (10,000 US dollars or more in any 12-month period, or 5% or more of gross income, or 5% or more ownership) include research grants from diagnostic and pharmaceutical companies to several members, speakers' bureau or honoraria relationships, and ownership interests for two members. Four members (Cercek, Drew, Hsue, Philippides) declare none. The reviewer disclosure table on p. 1905 lists three reviewers, all declaring none (p. 1904-1905).
funding.affiliations_note: The writing group are academic cardiologists and emergency physicians at US centres. One member is an author of several of the studies the statement relies on for incidence, prognosis and chest-pain-unit management. The declared industry relationships concern diagnostic and cardiovascular products rather than the generic drugs at issue in the recommendations; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the document.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of an intravenous beta blocker against the recommended alternatives in people presenting with chest pain after recent, confirmed cocaine use, with infarction, arrhythmia and death as outcomes, which would move both the beta-blocker and the labetalol recommendations off Level of Evidence C. Failing that, a guideline update that states, beside the Class III, how many people have actually received a beta blocker after cocaine in a controlled human study and under what conditions.

domains.note: A search is described, with a date range (1960 to 2007) and a list of targeted topics, which is more than most consensus documents offer, but no database is named, no search string or limits are given, no inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated and no study flow is reported. The search was English-language only. Beta blockers and labetalol, the subjects of the two Class III recommendations, are not among the named targeted searches.

No formal risk-of-bias assessment of any study, but the ACC/AHA class and level system is applied consistently, and the table on p. 1902 states for each therapy which kinds of evidence exist and how many patients they cover, which is a real and unusually transparent form of appraisal. What is missing is any comment on the internal limits of the key studies: that the catheterization participants had never used cocaine, and that in one of them the drug went directly into the coronary artery.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The incidence, prognosis and chest-pain-unit sections lean on the COCHPA study, a review of cocaine-induced infarction and the randomized observation-unit study, all of which involve one member of the writing group as an author. In a literature this small that is hard to avoid, and the statement does not conceal it, but the reader should know that several of its central numbers come from one group.

The therapeutics section opens by stating that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated infarction exists and that the recommendations rest on animal studies, catheterization studies, observational studies, case series and case reports. Mechanistic reasoning is labelled as such, uncertainty is stated where it exists (the role of calcium channel blockers is called uncertain, the appropriate diagnostic evaluation unclear), and the grading system attaches a level of evidence to every recommendation.

domains.domain: Balance of the evidence on beta-blockade, harm against safety
domains.note: The case for harm is set out in full (catheterization studies, case reports, animal models of seizure and death, esmolol raising blood pressure in up to 25% of patients) while nothing is offered on the other side, and the statement does not note that no human study had then examined clinical outcomes with or without a beta blocker. Much of this imbalance was a property of the 2007 literature rather than of the committee, and the statement partly corrects for it by printing the patient numbers; but a reader cannot tell from the text that only about 19 people had ever been given a beta blocker after cocaine under controlled conditions.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a professional body's consensus statement (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment cannot be milder than the worst domain, which is the unsystematic search. This is a better consensus document than most: it grades every recommendation, says plainly that no randomized trial of treatment exists, and prints the size and type of the evidence behind each therapy. It should be cited as the American Heart Association's 2008 judgment and for its statement of what that judgment rests on, including the Class III and Level C grades and the 30 and 15 patients in the table on p. 1902, never as independent evidence that beta blockers harm people who use cocaine. The numbers it reports from individual studies (incidence of infarction, complication rates, electrocardiogram performance) should be cited to those studies, which this encyclopedia appraises separately.

key_findings.finding: The statement grades beta blockers and labetalol Class III (evidence or general agreement that the treatment is not useful and in some cases may be harmful) at Level of Evidence C (consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care), against Class I Level B for benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin, Class I Level C for aspirin, and Class IIb Level C for calcium channel blockers and phentolamine.
key_findings.locator: Table, Classification of Recommendation / Level of Evidence column; definitions on p. 1897

key_findings.finding: The same table records the number of patients in the studies and reports behind each therapy: benzodiazepines 67, nitroglycerin 67, phentolamine 45, calcium channel blocker 15, beta blockers without alpha-blocking properties 30, labetalol 15, fibrinolytics 66.
key_findings.note: The 30 and the 15 are the enrolments of the two catheterization studies (Lange et al. 1990 and Boehrer et al. 1993). Editors' observation from those two papers, read in the same session: only 10 of the 30 and 9 of the 15 actually received a beta blocker after cocaine, so about 19 people in total; and in the 1990 study the propranolol was infused directly into the coronary artery rather than given systemically.

key_findings.finding: In the same table, beta blockers and labetalol are each marked as supported by cardiac catheterization laboratory studies, case reports and controlled in vivo animal experiments, with no mark under controlled clinical trials and none under case series or observational studies; only benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin carry a mark under controlled clinical trials.

The therapeutics section states that no randomized placebo-controlled trials of therapies to improve outcomes in cocaine-associated myocardial infarction have been reported, and that the recommendations are based on animal studies, cardiac catheterization studies, observational studies, case series and case reports.

The beta-blocker section states that coronary vasoconstriction is exacerbated by propranolol, that experimental models show beta-adrenergic antagonists decreasing coronary blood flow and increasing seizure frequency and mortality, that metoprolol has not been studied in cocaine-associated chest pain, that esmolol produced significant increases in blood pressure in up to 25% of patients, and that carvedilol has not been studied in this setting; it concludes that beta-adrenergic antagonists should be avoided in the acute setting.

The statement reasons that although beta blockers lower mortality after myocardial infarction unrelated to cocaine, deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, which alters the balance of risk and benefit.
key_findings.note: The supporting figure is the 0% in-hospital mortality in the 130-patient Cocaine-Associated Myocardial Infarction series cited on p. 1899.

key_findings.finding: On labetalol, the statement says it has substantially more beta- than alpha-adrenergic antagonist effect, increases the risk of seizure and death in animal models of cocaine toxicity, and does not reverse coronary artery vasoconstriction in humans, so it offers no advantage over propranolol.
key_findings.locator: Therapeutic Strategies > beta-Blockers, final paragraph (p. 1902) continuing at the top of p. 1903
key_findings.note: The human citation is Boehrer et al. 1993, in which 9 patients received labetalol.

key_findings.finding: At discharge, the statement advises that long-term beta-blocker use be reserved for those with the strongest indications (documented myocardial infarction, left ventricular systolic dysfunction or ventricular arrhythmias), individualized on a careful risk-benefit assessment and after counselling the patient about the interaction between recurrent cocaine use and beta-blockade, because recidivism is high.
key_findings.locator: Discharge Management and Secondary Prevention, final paragraph

key_findings.finding: Myocardial infarction occurred in 0.7% to 6% of patients presenting with chest pain after cocaine use across the cited studies: 6% in the COCHPA multicentre study of 246 patients and in a retrospective urban series, 2.8% in a series of 218, and 0.7% among 293 patients in the ACI-TIPI study; the statement attributes part of the variation to differences in diagnostic criteria and in the populations studied.

Among 130 patients with cocaine-associated myocardial infarction, 38% had cardiac complications, with heart failure in 7% and arrhythmias in up to 43% (ventricular tachycardia 18%, supraventricular tachycardia 5%, bradyarrhythmia 20%); 90% of complications occurred within the first 12 hours after presentation and in-hospital mortality was 0%.

The electrocardiogram performed poorly for detecting infarction in this population: in COCHPA, sensitivity 36%, specificity 89.9%, positive predictive value 17.9% and negative predictive value 95.8%; 56% to 84% of patients had an abnormal electrocardiogram, with early repolarization in 32% and left ventricular hypertrophy in 16% in one cohort of 101, and 42% of that cohort had ST-segment elevation although all had infarction excluded by cardiac markers.

In a prospective randomized study of 344 patients evaluated for cocaine-associated chest pain, 42 (12%) high-risk patients were admitted directly, of whom 10 (24%) had an infarction and 10 (24%) unstable angina; 302 intermediate- to low-risk patients were observed for 6 to 12 hours, among whom there were no cardiovascular deaths and 4 of 256 (2%) sustained a non-fatal infarction, and of the 158 (52%) who had a stress test before discharge only 4 (3%) were positive.
key_findings.locator: Evaluation in a Chest Pain Unit
key_findings.note: The statement draws from this its recommendation that intermediate- and low-risk patients can be managed in an observation unit for 9 to 12 hours and that stress testing be optional.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine use was reported as detectable in urine for about 24 to 48 hours after use, with a mean time to the first negative specimen of 43.6 +/- 17.1 hours (range 16 to 66) in 18 people who had used it intranasally, and as late as 22 days in people using large amounts long-term.
key_findings.note: This is the basis for the later observational studies' acknowledged inability to date cocaine use from a urine screen.

key_findings.finding: In the cardiac catheterization studies the statement relies on, intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg raised heart rate, blood pressure and coronary vascular resistance and narrowed coronary arterial diameter by 13%, and phentolamine returned the diameter to baseline.
key_findings.note: Reported as study conditions. The 13% figure is attributed to the 1989 study of the same Dallas group, not to Lange et al. 1990, whose Table 1 gives segment-by-segment falls of about 6% to 10%.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state that the article was reviewed by 4 outside reviewers nominated by the American Heart Association, while the reviewer disclosure table lists 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The extent of external review cannot be verified from the document. It bears on the evidence-report question of how independently the recommendations were checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The table of scientific strength has seven therapy rows (benzodiazepines, aspirin, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blocker, phentolamine, beta blockers, labetalol) but its footnote gives patient numbers for eight therapies, adding fibrinolytics, which has no row and no class or level of evidence in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 66 patients behind the fibrinolytic evidence cannot be matched to a graded recommendation; fibrinolysis is discussed in the text, where it is advised only for patients with ST-elevation infarction who cannot have percutaneous intervention.

reporting_issues.issue: The named targeted literature searches cover aspirin, nitroglycerin, calcium channel blockers, benzodiazepines, thrombolytics, phentolamine and heparin, but not beta blockers or labetalol, which are the two therapies the statement places in Class III.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot tell how the evidence behind the strongest negative recommendations was identified. Combined with the absence of named databases and search strings, this makes the search unreproducible.

reporting_issues.issue: The table counts 30 patients as the evidence base for beta blockers without alpha-blocking properties and 15 for labetalol. These are the full enrolments of the two cited catheterization studies; in those studies only 10 and 9 patients respectively received the beta blocker after cocaine, and in the 1990 study it was infused directly into the coronary artery rather than given systemically.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base for the Class III recommendations is smaller and narrower than the table's own figures suggest. Editors' observation from the two cited papers read in the same session; the statement itself does not mention the route or the number actually dosed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement attributes a 13% narrowing of coronary arterial diameter after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg to the 1989 study of the same group, while the 1990 study using the same dose reports segment-by-segment falls corresponding to about 6% to 10% and the 1993 study reports 13% +/- 10% across 40 segments in its abstract only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The single figure most often quoted for cocaine-induced coronary narrowing circulates without the sample, the segment or the spread behind it. A claim about the size of this effect should cite the primary table, not the statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The epidemiology section gives the 2004 national survey estimate as 14% of people aged 12 or over, which it equates to 34 million individuals in the United States, and separately reports more than 1.5 million Americans (0.6%) using cocaine in the past year in 2002 to 2003; reference 5 is marked deleted in proof.
reporting_issues.consequence: Lifetime and past-year figures are presented in the same paragraph from different survey years without the distinction being flagged in the sentence structure, and one supporting reference is missing from the list, so these prevalence figures should be taken from the surveys themselves rather than from this document.
